text: The worry is less that Cassini was filthy and more that it had instruments, tools, and possibly micro-organisms; Enceladus is a strong candidate for subsurface oceans, so you'd hate for a dead probe to end up smacking into it. With fuel running low, if the orbit had gone sideways it could have drifted into Enceladus or Titan, and nobody wanted to leave a spacecraft on a moon where you'd later be searching for life. They picked a final orbit that put it into Saturn's atmosphere, so it burned up rather than becoming a long-term impact hazard.

It's not really stationary. Even when you're rolling and not pushing, the leg that isn't doing the visible work is still bracing: your body is bouncing on the board, and your legs are absorbing bumps and keeping the deck from twisting. If you keep that leg locked or too rigid, the muscles around the knee, hip and ankle have to work hard to hold the position, so they can ache afterwards, especially the quad, hamstring or calf on that side.

For beginners it's common for one leg to feel sore because it's not used to the balance work. A slight bend in the knee and keeping the foot flat on the deck usually takes some of the strain. If it's the leg you use to push off, the hip flexors and knee may get tired from repeated pushes, but the question says stationary, so I'm assuming you mean the other leg. Don't treat the sore leg by standing perfectly straight; that just shifts all the load into one set of muscles, which is probably why it hurts when you stop.

The main thing is not to stand like a post. Skateboards don't move like bicycles, the deck can rock and slide under you, so you need micro adjustments constantly. That constant low-level muscle use is what aches, not a single injury. Give it a couple of days, keep the bend, and if the pain stays or comes from one clear spot near the knee or hip, then check footwear and board setup. If you're starting, one or two sessions aren't enough for the smaller muscles to adapt, so expect a bit of dull ache for a few days. But most of the time it's just your body learning to stay on a moving board with one leg doing less obvious work than it should.

The name is about ancestry, not where anyone was born or lived recently. For most African Americans, the link to Africa is historical, coming from the forced removal of enslaved people from the African continent to the colonies. So a Black person born in Baltimore or Chicago may never have set foot in Africa, but if their family line goes back to West Africa, Central Africa, or elsewhere on the continent, Afro-American is pointing at that ancestral connection, not a passport detail. It's similar to saying someone is American because their family has been here for generations; the label signals a cultural identity shaped in the US even when the origins are elsewhere. That doesn't make everyone African by birth or residence; it just names the shared roots. And no, it doesn't mean a current immigrant or direct country of origin; it's about the inherited connection. People also use African American, and older labels like Negro or Coloured carry their own histories, so the terms shift depending on who's speaking. The label is a rough shorthand, not a census line. It's a cultural and historical label, so it's okay if most people can't name an African country.

Syrians get weapons mostly through border crossings and smuggling routes from neighbours, plus what’s captured or handed out by factions and foreign backers. Lebanon, Turkey, Iraq and Gulf suppliers all matter, and seized guns and ammo are always moving around. They still get them because the state’s grip is patchy, so borders don’t fully stop small arms. It also helps that fighters, militias and local leaders benefit from having guns, which keeps the trade going. As far as I know, the practical effect is that even in quieter areas, weapons keep appearing where someone wants a fight.

The bit people don't get is that the brain's reward system isn't a pleasure switch. It's tied to alertness, pain, hunger, sex, social belonging, and a bunch of other housekeeping systems. That's why the drugs that give intense euphoria also tend to have real adverse effects: they're not making your brain feel good in isolation. They're pushing the same circuits that regulate heartbeat, breathing, muscle tone, and how much you want to keep using the substance.

With cocaine, you get the rush and the arousal, but you're also getting the jitter, the appetite drop, the insomnia, the kidney and heart strain, and the way your tolerance builds. Heroin does the opposite, which is why it feels good for pain and tension, but you also get sedation, constipation, and a withdrawal that can make your body feel awful for days. None of those are random. They're the same receptor networks doing their job, and the body is trying to hold itself in balance.

As far as I know, the deeper reason you can't just have the high without the cost is that strong pleasure usually means a dopamine surge, and the brain doesn't let those surges sit there. It downregulates the system to restore baseline. So the same mechanism that makes it pleasurable also makes your brain less sensitive to it. That's why a drug that worked too well would either be abused beyond sensible limits or would be tolerated by your body within days or weeks. Zero adverse effects would also mean zero natural braking. Your body has no built-in signal telling you to stop, and the result would be that everyone would use it constantly.

The other piece is that intense pleasure and intense dependence are often the same thing. The stronger the reward signal, the stronger the incentive to seek it again, and the more the system wants to compensate. So a drug that gave that same hit with literally no side effects would probably still be a problem, because the no adverse effects part would be misleading. You'd still get tolerance, cravings, and the pull to keep going.

I'd put it like this: the drugs on your list feel so good partly because they're disrupting multiple systems at once. You can't isolate one and leave the rest untouched. Even if you engineered the perfect pleasure, the brain would still want to compensate, which is a bit unfair.

Hi,

That pain is real, and I get it. A long day of shopping usually means hours on your feet, carrying bags, and trying to keep up with someone who can go for hours. Your body can end up with muscle tension, dehydration, or low energy, which shows up as that odd pressure around the head or a dull ache in the neck and shoulders. It's different from a normal headache because you're mixing physical strain with the stress of not wanting to seem a burden. I'd make sure you drink water and take breaks; if it keeps happening, it's worth mentioning to a doctor.

Thanks

I think that's just automatic association kicking in. You'd already been made to repeat and spell "silk" five times, so your brain was in a do-what-you're-told mode. Then "cows" is such a strong cue for "milk" that the first thing that popped out was milk, even though you know they drink water. The silk exercise didn't literally make you answer milk; it set up the same kind of automatic response, and the cow question tapped the most obvious association. You were probably in a state where your mind just grabbed the first strong link, and that link for cows is milk, not the factual answer water. It's an ordinary thing to happen after that sort of prompt. Your brother's little test wasn't checking whether you knew the fact, it was more like a prompt that made you respond in whatever pattern was already active. I wouldn't sweat it too much.
Thanks

Hi Anna,

I'm glad you're taking it slowly, because the house is the most expensive thing most of us will buy and the paperwork is the part that actually bites. For the property itself, don't just look at paint and flooring. Get a real inspector, and make the offer contingent on their report. Also pull the county property records and title report before you sign; you want to know about liens, easements, or a previous owner's unpaid taxes. If the seller refuses disclosure about leaks or an addition that wasn't permitted, that's a red flag.

On money, get pre-qualified first, but remember pre-qualification is not the same as underwriting. Ask your lender what the real monthly payment looks like with principal, interest, taxes, insurance, and HOA if any. If the house is a condo or part of an association, request the association's financials. I'd also look at comparable sales on that block over the last six months; the asking price is less reliable than you think if the comps are weak.

The biggest trap is falling in love with a place and then waiving the inspection contingency. That's how people end up paying to fix the roof, the electrical panel, or a bad septic system. Keep your offers contingent until you're comfortable.

Thanks,
Mark

The 3-in-1 is really a compromise formula; it has to work for skin, hair washing and conditioning at once, so none of those jobs is optimized the way a dedicated product would be. A 2-in-1 at least only balances two roles, which is why it tends to work better than a 3-in-1. The main difference from separate products is that individual ones can be formulated for one specific need, while the multi-task bottle uses a blend of surfactants and conditioning agents that is good enough for all three. I’ve tried the 3-in-1 before, and I wouldn’t bother with it for regular use; it’s a convenience item for travel or a quick wash, not a replacement for products made to do one job well. If you care about your hair or skin feeling properly cared for, separate shampoo and conditioner and body wash will usually beat it. That said, the 2-in-1 sits between: less compromised than the 3-in-1, but still not as targeted as dedicated products.

Thanks

Hi,

You leave GPS antennas on bedrock and record positions over days, months, years. The change in position is the speed. Modern GPS can resolve millimetre shifts, so a continent might move a few centimetres a year; that's about the same as a fingernail growing, which is why you need repeated measurements rather than just looking at the ground once.

For big plates, people compare many stations to see the pattern, and use satellite data and seismological information to understand plate motion. But for the actual speed, it's mostly geodetic positioning: where the point is now, where it was before, and how fast it is going.

You don't need a lot of machinery. A small GPS base station, a fixed reference, and patience. In my experience, the boring part is waiting for consistent baselines, because the ground and the reference frame are never entirely stable. That's why people use many stations and long time series rather than one quick snapshot. A year of data helps separate real plate motion from local ground effects, and a decade of data is much more useful for the average speed. The slow, careful measurements are what make the speed usable over long periods.

Thanks
S.

Inbreeding raises the chance that a child inherits the same rare harmful variant from both parents. In a small or related family, many harmful mutations are carried silently, because one normal copy usually masks them. When two related people have a child, shared ancestry means both may carry the same variant, so the child may get two copies and the effect appears.

IQ is shaped by many genes and by environment, but many small genetic effects can add up. That is why related parents may have a child with lower IQ than average; the genetics are more exposed, not a brand new mutation. This is not a single-gene story, and not every child of related parents will have lower IQ. The key idea is that inbreeding makes hidden recessive variants more likely to show; recessive means a genetic effect is masked by a normal copy.

This isn't because arms are magically tougher. Nerve endings aren't evenly spread across your body. The face, hands, and tongue have far more pain-sensing cells, so a small scratch there stings badly. Much of the forearm and upper arm has relatively fewer sensitive endings, and it carries a layer of fat and muscle that cushions a hit or a small penetration.

That's why a jab to the arm can feel like a bump while the same force on the ribs or face feels worse. But don't assume an arm injury is minor. If it hits a nerve, tendon, artery, or bone, the pain can be sharp and sudden.

The 'seems less' part is also psychological. A wound to a limb feels remote from your core, so your brain may treat it as less threatening than one near the chest or head. The difference is nerve density, padding, and how dangerous your brain judges the site to be.

The main difference is what each gas does to your blood. Carbon monoxide sticks to the oxygen-carrying protein in red cells about 200 times more strongly than oxygen does. It forms a compound called carboxyhemoglobin, and the protein doesn't let go of it easily, so your blood is left with much less capacity to move oxygen to the brain and other organs. That's why CO poisoning hits fast: the brain is starved of oxygen, and the symptoms—headache, confusion, dizziness, then loss of consciousness—follow that sequence.

Carbon dioxide is a different matter. It is a normal waste product of your body's metabolism. Your cells produce it, your blood carries it, and your lungs exhale it. Under ordinary conditions, you produce and remove it continuously, so it is not poisonous in the way carbon monoxide is. People sometimes assume CO2 must be more dangerous because we breathe it, but at everyday levels your body is already built to handle it.

What makes CO tricky in practice is that it is colourless and has no smell. You cannot notice it until the effects show up in your head, by which time the blood's oxygen carriage is already compromised. CO2 at very high concentrations can also be dangerous, because it pushes oxygen out of the air and changes the acidity of your blood, but that's not the usual comparison. The everyday rule is simple: CO quietly cuts off oxygen delivery, while CO2 is just part of the normal exhaust you breathe out.

If a plane hits the ground or is struck by an object, the aircraft stops or changes direction suddenly, but your body keeps moving. The brace position helps by bringing you into a compact shape and keeping your head low. You lower your head, bend your neck, put your arms in front of your chest or hold your hands near your head, and press your feet flat on the floor. That shape does two things: it reduces how far your head and chest can move forward, and it keeps your neck from snapping.

This matters most in a hard landing or collision, where the biggest risks are head, neck, and chest injuries. A firm floor or seat frame under your feet gives your legs a place to absorb some of the force. You are not trying to make yourself small for its own sake; you are limiting the part of your body that is most vulnerable. In practice, the position is simple to learn, but it only helps if you know when to do it, and stay in it. Cabin crew will call for brace, or you will see passengers and crew already in it, and that is the cue.

Most consumer brands are children of industrialisation. You need factories, standardised goods, and mass advertising to make a name familiar to millions, and those things mostly show up in the 19th and 20th centuries. That's why Coca-Cola, Nestlé, and Disney are household names: they started after the industrial era began, when companies could produce at scale and reach a wider audience. Pre-industrial firms stayed small, local, and tied to a craft, so they didn't build the recognition we call a brand today. A few old names do exist, but the famous ones are products of the industrial era's own scale.

I keep seeing this exact question because it trips people up: the dealer advertises a lower rate, but the total cost can still be lower with a bank. The headline interest rate is not the whole bill. Dealerships can quote a very low or even zero percent promotional rate, but that rate is usually tied to a vehicle price that is higher than the bank route, plus fees for documentation, origination, and dealer add-ons. I take the position that a bank is often cheaper because you negotiate the cash price, take a normal bank loan, and avoid the dealer’s packaging. The bank’s higher nominal rate does not automatically mean a higher total cost, because the bank loan is run on a lower principal.

Say you are looking at a $30,000 car. A dealer offers it at 2.9% for 72 months. That looks attractive, but the dealer may add $1,200 in fees, a $900 warranty, and a $600 dealer installation charge before the loan starts. On the bank route, the same car may be bought at a negotiated $27,000, financed at 5.4% for 60 months, with modest bank fees. Even though the bank’s rate is higher, the lower loan amount and shorter term can make the total interest plus fees lower. The dealer’s low rate on a larger principal does not save money.

This is why I stop comparing rates and start comparing what I would actually pay out the door. Dealers know a low rate draws buyers in. That’s a marketing tactic, not a guarantee of a good deal. A bank, by contrast, usually sells a plain loan with fewer bundled charges. If the dealer’s financing includes add-ons you did not ask for, or the vehicle price is padded, the bank route can be the cheaper one even when its rate looks worse.

The practical rule I use is simple. Get the dealer’s itemized out-the-door cost, then ask the bank for a cash discount and a loan quote. Compare the sum of principal, interest, and fees, not the advertised percentage. That is how you see through the lower dealer rate. In many cases, the bank’s slightly higher APR ends up costing less because the dealership’s lower rate is buried under extra charges and a higher car price. I would not let a glossy dealer sheet decide the answer. The question is whether the total payments and fees make the bank loan cheaper, and in my experience that is often the case.

It's a mess, but I still side with legalization, with conditions. A state can make it legal while the federal government still calls it illegal, which is the kind of inconsistency that leaves people confused and sometimes in trouble. A person can buy a brownie in a recreational state, then drive into a state with stricter rules and wonder what's happening. That's not a theoretical problem.

My position is that adults should have the choice to use it, but not the choice to use it while operating a truck or a car. The details matter: how much, how recently, and whether it's being sold in tiny packages with no label. I'd rather have sensible rules and clear limits than a state-by-state guessing game. If we're going to legalize it, we should also fix the federal gap before calling it settled. And until the two systems line up, the map stays confusing.

I still find it a little strange that my own body runs on chemistry that looks a lot like tiny batteries. Cells keep sodium and potassium ions unevenly distributed across their membranes, and that difference creates voltage. When a nerve or muscle cell gets the signal to fire, ion channels open, sodium rushes in, the voltage flips for a brief moment, and that's the electricity we're feeling in a heartbeat, a twitch, a thought. I take the position that the body doesn't generate a separate current; it's the movement of ions, not magic sparks. It's messy, chemical, and surprisingly reliable.

I keep saying I'm a musician who has released a few tracks, and the one thing I never expect from people is how much they think the sampling itself is the interesting part. They hear a track where someone has flipped a 1960s horn line or looped a breakbeat and they ask "how did they do that?" I did a sample last year, and I'm not ashamed to say the creative bit took me an afternoon. The legal bit took about a week, which is the part nobody warns you about.

When you sample an older song you're cutting a snippet of the original and dropping it into your arrangement, usually with pitch, tempo and effects shifted. Queen's "Another One Bites the Dust" is a clean example; it was built around a sampled drum break rather than a live kit, and the effect is still recognisable. But the technical act is almost secondary now. The real gate is clearing two separate sets of rights: the composition (the melody and lyrics as written) and the master recording (the actual performance). Those are often owned by different companies, and if the writer's publisher and the record label can't agree on money, your track is stuck. A sample fee can be structured as a one-off payment or a share of sales, and even a two-second snippet can trigger a clearance obligation.

This is where I get a little bitter. You can spend months on a beat and then lose a week to the licensing step because the publisher for a 1971 song is inside a big conglomerate, and they'll want a share of future royalties instead of a flat fee. Finding the rights holder is its own job; the original artist is often dead or the label is defunct, and the composition might sit with a publisher that changed owners three times. Some producers I know now budget the sample fee into the project from day one rather than treating it as an afterthought. I think that's the actual lesson: a sampled track is really a negotiation with three parties, and the most expensive thing is the waiting, not the money.

I'm not saying you can't sample older songs. You can. I'm saying people get the emphasis wrong. The flip is the fun part; the clearance is the part that decides whether your track gets released at all. Next time someone asks how it's done, I tell them: the technical answer is "you loop it," but the real answer is "you clear it."

Why does your head hurt? Well, the brain itself doesn't actually feel pain, which is a bit confusing since people tend to blame their thoughts for a physical ache. The pain is coming from the tension building up in the muscles at the back of your neck, or the blood vessels around the brain expanding and pressing on the sensitive tissues (the meninges). As far as I know, it's mostly a muscle or vascular issue. I wouldn't spend too much time analyzing it; just relax the jaw and neck, which is usually where the real culprit sits. It's kind of annoying that the actual pain is so hard to pin down, but the body knows what it's doing. I find that sitting too long in front of a screen is the main trigger for me, and the pain starts in the scalp and radiates out. No idea why people keep overthinking it.

I can't even tell you if the food was good because we never got to eat. We arrived at 7:20 p.m. on Sunday and picked this place because we had a 10:00 p.m. show in the same hotel, so figured it'd be easy. We entered our names into their completely useless digital waitlist and were told to come back to pay at 8:23 p.m. We did, but then stood around until 8:40 p.m., when staff casually mentioned we probably wouldn't be seated until 9:15 p.m. We were a party of two, and they offered zero solutions. If the wait stretches that far past payment, tell people upfront so our night isn't completely wasted. Absolute disaster; zero stars if that were an option.

I went to this buffet on a Friday around 4:30 p.m., and surprisingly, there really was no line at all. For two, it came out to about $130, which felt pretty steep. Going in, I’d assumed the price would be comparable to a steakhouse, and afterward I learned it actually cost a bit more than I’d expected to pay at one. I was disappointed that steak wasn’t on the menu; at that price, I figured there’d be some kind of steak option. The meat choices were lamb, prime rib, and chicken, but those are things I feel like you can find at other Las Vegas buffets for much less.

The seafood station had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan crab legs are available at a lot of Vegas buffets, but I hadn’t run into rock crab claws anywhere else, so those were interesting. The problem was that there were no crab crackers. Staff said wooden mallets were available, but our table was so close to the next one that I didn’t want to start smashing the crab shells and send bits flying at the people next to us. So I just ate the crab legs. The Asian station didn’t stand out either, and it reminded me a lot of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert had gelato and various pastries, but nothing really stood out. They also had fresh juices, though I didn’t try any.

Overall, I’d call the buffet acceptable but overpriced for what it offers. If you’re curious, it’s worth trying once, especially if there’s no wait. But if the line is long, I’d probably reconsider.

★★★★☆ Keeping it

The space bar rattles; hit it with the edge of your thumb and it sounds like a loose pen cap in a drawer. The E key also repeats now and then, so "example" becomes "eexample" and I have to backspace. It happens maybe once an afternoon, always when I'm typing fast and not looking.

I paid $38 and kept it anyway, actually because of the switches. When I asked the seller what they were, the answer took a week. By then I had already pulled off a keycap and found out for myself: brown tactile switches, with a small bump under the finger and a soft landing at the bottom. My old membrane board felt like pressing wet cardboard by comparison.

I mostly email, often two or three hours in a row, and my wrists don't ache by the end anymore. That mattered more than the rattle.

Sending it back would have meant paying for postage and boxing it up, and I'd have been stuck without a keyboard while I waited. So it still stays on the desk, and I tap the space bar a little closer to the middle now.

I've been going to Vegas pretty much my whole life (well, the under-21 version of it), so I've sat through a lot of shows before I could even gamble. Le Rêve at the Wynn is one I finally caught, and I'd call it mixed, maybe worse than mixed.

The circular stage is genuinely smart. You're looking down into it, so from essentially any seat you get a decent view, which is rare in Vegas. The individual acts are impressive; the strength stuff, the aerialists, the divers. Those people are athletes, no question. But a lot of it reminded me of Cirque du Soleil. Not in a rip-off way, just that if you've seen Cirque, you've seen comparable feats done with more clarity.

Clarity is the problem. What is the story? I still don't know. There's a dream, maybe? A guy, or maybe just water? It felt like a bunch of pretty images thrown at you, and the show never tells you what it's trying to say. Also, there's way too much happening at once. Too many people, too many elements, too many "wow" moments stacked on top of each other. A more restrained production would hit harder. This felt like the stereotypical Vegas spectacle thing, where more is better, so they crammed everything in.

One practical ticket note: if you're staying at Wynn or Encore, they have a deal ($99 instead of the normal $125). That helps a lot. I wouldn't pay for it a second time. Apart from a few stunts, it was just average. I wasn't blown away, and I don't think anyone else was either. That said, a few friends liked it. If you've never seen it before, maybe check it out, just don't expect to leave overwhelmed.

About two years ago we ordered two shirts for my father from Rockmount Ranch Wear over the phone. They never arrived because the salesperson recorded the delivery address incorrectly; her handwritten 7 was taken as a 1, so the intended 5407 was sent to 5401. The residents of 5401 brought the package to the local UPS store for return, after which it disappeared and we never heard another word about it. We didn’t find out until several weeks later. During the dispute we placed an extra order for two shirts, and Rockmount refused to refund the original pair. The owner handled it at that point. He acknowledged the shipment went to the wrong address but said no refund until the shirts were returned. He also said we were partly to blame for not being friendly enough to the residents at 5401, four doors away. We disputed the original charge with our credit-card company and eventually got a credit.
